name: Design an Ad Click Aggregation Pipeline
intent: Count billions of ad clicks per day into per-ad, per-minute totals that advertisers can see within a minute and be billed on, even though clicks arrive late, out of order, twice and from bots.
codeTitle: event-time windows with a watermark and click-id dedup
finalIntro: One click, from a phone to a billed total.
prompt: Design the system that counts clicks on ads for an advertising platform. Advertisers want the number of clicks per ad per minute, in a dashboard that is fresh within about a minute, and the same numbers are used to bill them. Clicks come from phones and browsers over unreliable networks, some arrive late or twice, some are fake, and a few ads get a huge share of the traffic.
functional: Record every click on an ad with the ad, the time it happened and who clicked
Report clicks per ad in one-minute windows, and roll them up to hours and days
Answer queries such as the clicks of one ad in the last hour, or the top 100 ads in the last 10 minutes
Count each real click exactly once, even if it is sent or processed more than once
Exclude fraudulent and duplicate clicks from the billed totals
Correct a total after the fact when a late click or a fraud review changes it
nonFunctional: Handle an average of about 6,000 clicks per second, and 20,000 or more at the peak
Dashboard numbers are fresh within about a minute, and the final billed number may take hours
Never lose a click that the advertiser could be billed for
Billed totals must be accurate, so what is shown quickly may be corrected later
Survive the loss of any single machine without losing or double counting clicks
Stay balanced when one ad receives a large share of all clicks

firstAttempt.text: The click endpoint runs one SQL statement per click: it inserts a row into a clicks table and adds one to a counter row for the ad and the current minute. A report is a query on the counter table.
limits: Thousands of updates per second to the same few counter rows queue up behind row locks, and a viral ad makes one row the bottleneck of the whole system
The minute is the time the server received the click, so a click delayed by a bad network is counted in the wrong minute
A retry after a timeout adds one again, and nothing tells a repeat from a new click
If the database is slow the endpoint is slow, and clicks are lost while it is down
Bots and double clicks are counted as real, and there is no way to recompute the numbers once they are added

steps.title: Write every click to a durable log first
steps.problem: Counting in the request path ties the endpoint to a database that cannot take the write rate, and a click that is not stored when it arrives is gone for good.
steps.fix: A stateless collector validates the click, which carries an id and the time it happened, and appends it to a partitioned, replicated log such as Kafka, keyed by the ad id. It answers as soon as the log has acknowledged the write. Counting now happens behind the log, at its own pace, and the log keeps the raw clicks for days so that anything downstream can be rebuilt by reading it again.
steps.tradeoff: The endpoint is fast and a slow or failed counter no longer loses clicks, because the log absorbs the burst. There is a new system to run, and the counts now trail the clicks by a short delay.

steps.title: Aggregate in windows of event time
steps.problem: A counter row per ad and minute is hot, and the minute should be the minute when the click happened, not when the server happened to see it.
steps.fix: A stream processor reads each partition, groups clicks by ad and by the minute of the time stamped on the click (the event time), and keeps a running count per window in memory, saving its state to disk at regular checkpoints. A tumbling window is a fixed minute that does not overlap with the next. Only a finished total, or an update to it, is written to the aggregate store, so the store sees one write per ad per window instead of one per click. A question such as 'the last hour' is answered by adding up sixty one-minute totals, which is a sliding window built from tumbling ones.
steps.tradeoff: Totals are right by the time of the click, and the store takes a tiny, steady load. The processor now holds state that must survive a restart, and a window cannot be called final while clicks for it may still be on their way.

steps.title: Close windows with a watermark, and handle late clicks
steps.problem: Clicks arrive out of order, because networks, retries and offline phones delay them. If a window is closed too early, clicks are lost, and if it never closes, the number is never final.
steps.fix: The processor tracks a watermark: the newest event time it has seen, minus an allowed lateness such as 30 seconds. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window is final and its total is written. A click for a window that has already closed is not discarded. It goes to a late-events output, and a correction is applied to the stored total, either as an increment or by recomputing the window.
steps.tradeoff: The allowed lateness is a dial between speed and completeness: a short one gives fast but slightly low numbers, and a long one gives complete numbers later. Late corrections mean the dashboard must accept that a shown number can still go up.

steps.title: Count each click once with an id
steps.problem: A phone that gets no reply resends the click, a consumer that crashes re-reads part of the log, and both would count the same click again. Billing cannot tolerate that.
steps.fix: Every click has an id that the client side cannot change by retrying, such as a signed token issued when the ad was shown, so all retries carry the same id. The aggregator remembers the ids it has counted, in a store with an expiry just longer than the lateness it accepts, and ignores an id it has seen. Counting is at least once from the log, and the id check, together with checkpoints that save the offsets and the counts together, makes the result behave as if it were exactly once.
steps.tradeoff: A duplicate, whether it comes from the network or from replay, is counted at most once. The id store has to hold every id for the retention period, which is a lot of memory at this rate, and a duplicate that arrives after the expiry is counted again.

steps.title: Spread a hot ad over many workers
steps.problem: Keying by ad sends every click of one ad to one partition. When an ad goes viral it overloads that partition's worker while the others are idle, and adding workers does not help.
steps.fix: A pre-aggregator adds up clicks in small batches and splits a hot ad into several sub-keys by adding a salt, such as ad-42#0 to ad-42#7, so its clicks are spread across several workers. Each worker produces a partial count per window, and a second stage merges the partials for the same ad and window. Only ads known to be hot need the salt, found from a short-term counter of the busiest keys. Pre-adding in each worker also turns thousands of clicks into one message.
steps.tradeoff: The busiest ad no longer limits the throughput, and the merge is cheap since there are only a handful of partials. A second stage adds a little delay, and the salt for a hot ad must be handled the same way by every producer and by the merge.

steps.title: Filter fraud, and reconcile with a batch recount
steps.problem: Bots, click farms and double clicks inflate counts that advertisers pay for, and the streaming numbers, produced fast with a short lateness, are not good enough to bill on.
steps.fix: A fraud filter in front of the log drops what is clearly invalid, such as clicks without a valid signed token or with impossible speed, and flags the rest, using per-device and per-address rates and a score that is improved offline. The raw clicks are also kept in an archive. A batch job recounts each finished day from the archive, with the full lateness, the final fraud rules and exact dedup, and overwrites the streaming totals for that day. The billed number is the batch number. That is the lambda design, a fast path and a correct path. A kappa design has only the stream and fixes a number by replaying the log through the same code.
steps.tradeoff: Advertisers see a fast estimate and are billed on a correct number, and a rule change can be applied to old data. There are two paths to keep in agreement, or in a kappa design one path whose replay of a long period is slow and costly, and fraud rules can wrongly remove real clicks.

failures.scenario: The stream processor crashes in the middle of a window
failures.impact: The counts held in memory are lost, and after a restart the clicks since the last checkpoint could be counted twice or not at all.
failures.answer: State and log offsets are saved together at each checkpoint. After the restart the processor loads the last checkpoint and reads the log again from the saved offset, so every click after it is processed once more. The click id store turns any repeat into a no-op, and the writes to the store set the total for a window rather than add to it.

failures.scenario: A mobile network outage delivers an hour of clicks all at once
failures.impact: The clicks are far behind the watermark, so they are late for windows that are already final, and they arrive as a burst.
failures.answer: The late-events output takes them without disturbing the live path, and a correction job applies them to the right windows as increments. Anything older than the dedup retention is held for the nightly batch recount, which sees them in the archive with their real event times. The log buffers the burst, and the processor catches up without losing anything.

failures.scenario: One ad goes viral during a live event
failures.impact: Its clicks are over a third of the traffic, and the worker that owns the key falls behind while the others are idle, so the dashboard and the billing lag.
failures.answer: The key is salted into several sub-keys and its clicks are pre-added before the shuffle, so the load is spread over many workers and merged in a cheap second stage. Alerts on consumer lag per partition show the problem early, and the hot key list is updated automatically.

failures.scenario: A click farm sends a million fake clicks on a competitor's ad
failures.impact: The advertiser would be billed for clicks that no customer made, and would lose trust in the platform.
failures.answer: The filter blocks clicks without a valid signed token and rates clicks per device and address. The ones that get through are caught by the offline scoring, and the batch recount removes them with the final rules before the invoice is made. The advertiser is credited for any click found invalid after billing.

alternatives.title: Architecture: lambda or kappa

options.name: Lambda: a stream for speed and a batch for truth
options.pro: The batch can be exact and simple, and it fixes anything the stream got wrong
options.con: Two code bases that must give the same answer, and a team to run both

options.name: Kappa: one stream, with replay for fixes
options.pro: One code base and one set of semantics
options.con: Replaying months of clicks through the stream is slow and expensive, and the stream must be exact

alternatives.pick: A stream with a short lateness for the dashboard, plus a daily batch recount for billing. Share the counting logic between the two where possible, and treat the batch figure as the one that is billed.

alternatives.title: Window type

options.name: Tumbling (fixed, no overlap)
options.pro: Each click is in exactly one window, which is cheap and easy to correct
options.con: Reports are only in whole windows

options.name: Sliding (overlapping)
options.pro: A smooth 'last hour' that updates every minute
options.con: Each click belongs to many windows, so the work and the state multiply

alternatives.pick: Tumbling one-minute windows as the unit of storage, and sliding or longer windows computed by adding minutes at query time.

alternatives.title: How to deduplicate

options.name: Exact id set with an expiry
options.pro: Never wrong inside the retention period
options.con: Memory in proportion to the clicks in the period

options.name: Bloom filter
options.pro: A very small amount of memory
options.con: A false positive drops a real click that should have been billed

options.name: Rely on idempotent writes only
options.con: Works for repeated writes of a total, not for the same click arriving as two events

alternatives.pick: An exact id set with an expiry in the stream, and an exact distinct count in the batch recount.

alternatives.title: How long to wait for late clicks

options.name: Short (seconds)
options.pro: Windows finalise quickly and state is small
options.con: More clicks arrive after their window closed and need corrections

options.name: Long (minutes)
options.pro: Almost no late clicks are missed
options.con: The first complete number is delayed and more windows are held in memory

alternatives.pick: Wait about 30 seconds for the live number, accept corrections for a few minutes, and let the batch recount catch all the rest.
